title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
description: Class 12 Chemistry notes on aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids: structure, preparation, nucleophilic addition, aldol, Cannizzaro, Tollens and acidity order.

topics.title: Carbonyl Compounds: Structure & Preparation
topics.concept:
Aldehydes and ketones both contain the carbonyl group (>C=O), so they are together called carbonyl compounds. In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen (general formula R–CHO), while in a ketone the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms (R–CO–R'). The simplest aldehyde is methanal (HCHO, formaldehyde) and the simplest ketone is propanone (CH3COCH3, acetone).

Nomenclature

In IUPAC names the aldehyde group is denoted by the suffix -al and the longest chain is numbered so the –CHO carbon is C-1 (e.g. CH3CH2CHO is propanal; CH3CH(CH3)CHO is 2-methylpropanal). Ketones take the suffix -one with a locant for the carbonyl carbon (CH3COCH2CH3 is butan-2-one). Common names of aldehydes derive from the acid (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde); ketones are named as alkyl/aryl + ketone (ethyl methyl ketone). Benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO) and acetophenone (C6H5COCH3) are common aromatic members.

Structure & nature of the carbonyl group

The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised; the three σ-bonds lie in a plane at about 120° and the unhybridised p-orbital overlaps sideways with a p-orbital of oxygen to give the π-bond. Because oxygen is far more electronegative than carbon, the π-electrons are pulled towards oxygen, making the bond strongly polar: the carbon is electron-poor (δ+) and the oxygen electron-rich (δ−). This polarity, written C=O ↔ +C–O−, controls all of carbonyl chemistry — the δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles and the δ− oxygen by electrophiles/acids. The polar C=O also gives these compounds appreciable dipole moments and higher boiling points than non-polar hydrocarbons of similar mass.

Methods of preparation

(a) By oxidation of alcohols. Primary alcohols give aldehydes (e.g. with PCC, pyridinium chlorochromate, which stops at the aldehyde stage); secondary alcohols give ketones (with acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7). (b) By dehydrogenation of alcohols over hot Cu at 573 K: 1° alcohols → aldehydes, 2° alcohols → ketones. (c) From acyl chlorides (Rosenmund reduction): RCOCl + H2 → RCHO over Pd poisoned with BaSO4 to prevent over-reduction. (d) From nitriles and esters: nitriles on partial reduction (Stephen reaction, SnCl2/HCl, then H2O) or with DIBAL-H give aldehydes; esters with DIBAL-H also give aldehydes. (e) From hydrocarbons: ozonolysis of alkenes yields aldehydes/ketones depending on substitution; Gattermann–Koch reaction converts benzene to benzaldehyde with CO + HCl/anhydrous AlCl3–CuCl. (f) Friedel–Crafts acylation: an aromatic ring + RCOCl/anhydrous AlCl3 gives an aryl ketone (e.g. benzene + CH3COCl → acetophenone).

Physical properties

Lower members are colourless liquids (methanal is a gas) with characteristic odours. They cannot form intermolecular H-bonds among themselves (no O–H), so their boiling points are lower than the corresponding alcohols/acids but higher than comparable hydrocarbons/ethers because of dipole–dipole attraction. Lower aldehydes and ketones are fairly soluble in water (H-bonding with water through the carbonyl O), the solubility falling as the hydrocarbon part grows.

examples.problem: Give the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO and of CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
examples.solution:
1. The first compound has a four-carbon chain ending in –CHO; number from the CHO carbon (C-1).
  2. Chain of 4 carbons with the -al suffix → butanal.
  3. The second has a four-carbon chain with C=O on C-2: butan-2-one.

Answer: Butanal and butan-2-one.

examples.problem: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to an aldehyde without over-oxidising it to a carboxylic acid, and why?
examples.solution:
1. Acidified KMnO4/K2Cr2O7 oxidise the aldehyde further to the acid.
  2. PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in CH2Cl2 is a mild, anhydrous oxidant.
  3. It stops at the aldehyde because no water is present to form the hydrate that gets over-oxidised.

Answer: PCC; it is a mild anhydrous oxidant that halts oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

examples.problem: How is benzaldehyde prepared directly from benzene? Name the reaction and reagents.
examples.solution:
1. Benzene cannot be formylated by an acyl halide of formic acid (it is unstable).
  2. Use a mixture of CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl3 (and CuCl).
  3. This in-situ generates the formyl cation; it attacks the ring.

Answer: Gattermann–Koch reaction: C6H6 + CO + HCl ⟶(anhyd. AlCl3/CuCl) C6H5CHO.

examples.problem: Write the product when acetyl chloride (CH<sub>3</sub>COCl) is treated with H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/BaSO<sub>4</sub>. Name the reaction.
examples.solution:
1. An acyl chloride reduced by H2 on a poisoned Pd catalyst gives an aldehyde.
  2. BaSO4 (plus S/quinoline) poisons Pd so reduction stops at –CHO.
  3. CH3COCl + H2 → CH3CHO + HCl.

Answer: Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) by Rosenmund reduction.

examples.problem: What carbonyl products form on ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
examples.solution:
1. Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C double bond.
  2. The (CH3)2C= fragment has no H on the doubly bonded carbon → ketone (propanone).
  3. The =CHCH3 fragment has one H → aldehyde (ethanal).

Answer: Propanone (acetone) and ethanal (acetaldehyde).

examples.problem: Arrange propanal, propan-1-ol and butane in increasing order of boiling point and justify.
examples.solution:
1. Butane is non-polar (only weak van der Waals forces) — lowest b.p.
  2. Propanal is polar (dipole–dipole) but has no O–H, so no intermolecular H-bonding — intermediate.
  3. Propan-1-ol forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds — highest b.p.

Answer: butane < propanal < propan-1-ol.

recap: Carbonyl group >C=O has an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon (~120°) and is strongly polar (C is δ+, O is δ−).
Aldehydes (R–CHO, suffix -al) have H on the carbonyl carbon; ketones (R–CO–R', suffix -one) have two C.
Oxidation/dehydrogenation of 1° alcohols → aldehydes, 2° alcohols → ketones.
Rosenmund (RCOCl + H<sub>2</sub>/Pd-BaSO<sub>4</sub>) and Stephen/DIBAL-H (from nitriles/esters) make aldehydes; Gattermann–Koch makes benzaldehyde; Friedel–Crafts acylation makes aryl ketones.
No self H-bonding, so b.p. lower than alcohols/acids but higher than hydrocarbons; lower members are water-soluble.

quiz.q: The carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde is:
quiz.explanation: It forms three sigma bonds in a plane (~120°) and one pi bond, so it is sp<sup>2</sup>.

quiz.q: Rosenmund reduction of an acyl chloride uses:
quiz.explanation: The Pd catalyst is poisoned by BaSO<sub>4</sub> so reduction stops at the aldehyde.

quiz.q: Which reaction converts benzene into benzaldehyde using CO and HCl with anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>/CuCl?
quiz.explanation: Gattermann–Koch formylates benzene directly with CO + HCl.

quiz.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a:
quiz.explanation: A 2° alcohol has the OH on a carbon bearing two C groups, so oxidation yields a ketone.

topics.title: Reactions of Aldehydes & Ketones
topics.concept:
Because the carbonyl carbon is electron-poor (δ+), the central reaction of aldehydes and ketones is nucleophilic addition. A nucleophile attacks the planar carbon, which rehybridises from sp2 to sp3, and the oxygen accepts the electron pair to give a tetrahedral alkoxide that is then protonated.

Important nucleophilic additions

(a) HCN adds to give a cyanohydrin (R2C(OH)CN), a useful route to α-hydroxy acids. (b) NaHSO3 gives a crystalline bisulphite addition product used to purify and separate aldehydes/methyl ketones. (c) Alcohols add (with dry HCl) to give hemiacetals and then acetals [R–CH(OR')2], a common way of protecting the carbonyl group. (d) Ammonia derivatives (NH2–Z) add and then lose water to give C=N compounds: hydroxylamine → oximes, hydrazine → hydrazones, phenylhydrazine → phenylhydrazones, and 2,4-DNP → orange 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones (a test for the carbonyl group).

Relative reactivity: aldehyde vs ketone

Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition for two reasons: (i) steric — an aldehyde has only one bulky group plus a small H, so the nucleophile reaches the carbon easily; (ii) electronic — the two alkyl groups of a ketone are electron-donating (+I), reducing the δ+ on carbon and stabilising the reactant. Hence the order is HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3.

Oxidation and reduction

Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids (even by mild reagents); ketones resist oxidation and break only under vigorous conditions. Reduction to alcohols uses NaBH4 or LiAlH4 (or H2/Ni): aldehyde → 1° alcohol, ketone → 2° alcohol. Reduction all the way to the –CH2– (alkane) is done by Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl, acidic) or Wolff–Kishner reduction (NH2NH2 then KOH/glycol, basic).

Reactions due to α-hydrogen

The H on the carbon next to C=O (the α-H) is acidic because the resulting carbanion (enolate) is resonance-stabilised. Aldol condensation: two molecules of an aldehyde/ketone bearing α-H combine in dilute base to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl (an aldol), which on heating loses water to give an α,β-unsaturated product. A cross-aldol uses two different carbonyl partners (useful only when the choice of products is controlled, e.g. one partner has no α-H).

Cannizzaro reaction

Aldehydes with no α-H (e.g. HCHO, C6H5CHO) undergo self oxidation–reduction (disproportionation) in concentrated alkali: one molecule is reduced to an alcohol and another oxidised to the carboxylate salt.

Tests for distinction

Tollens' test: aldehydes reduce ammoniacal AgNO3 to a silver mirror; ketones do not. Fehling's test: aliphatic aldehydes give a red-brown Cu2O precipitate; aromatic aldehydes and ketones do not. Iodoform test: compounds with a CH3CO– group (or CH3CH(OH)–) give a yellow CHI3 precipitate with I2/NaOH — positive for acetaldehyde and methyl ketones, negative for other aldehydes/ketones.

examples.problem: Why is acetaldehyde more reactive than acetone towards HCN addition?
examples.solution:
1. Nucleophilic addition is favoured by a more δ+ and less hindered carbonyl carbon.
  2. Acetone has two electron-donating CH3 groups (+I) that lower δ+ and crowd the carbon.
  3. Acetaldehyde has only one CH3 and a small H, so it is less hindered and more electrophilic.

Answer: Acetaldehyde is more reactive due to lower steric hindrance and a higher δ+ on its carbonyl carbon.

examples.problem: Write the aldol product and the final α,β-unsaturated product when ethanal undergoes aldol condensation.
examples.solution:
1. Dilute NaOH removes an α-H of one CH3CHO to give the enolate.
  2. The enolate adds to the carbonyl C of a second CH3CHO → aldol: CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO (3-hydroxybutanal).
  3. On heating it loses water → CH3CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal).

Answer: Aldol = 3-hydroxybutanal; final product = but-2-enal (after –H2O).

examples.problem: Benzaldehyde is treated with concentrated NaOH. What happens and why?
examples.solution:
1. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot do an aldol.
  2. With concentrated alkali it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction (disproportionation).
  3. One molecule is reduced to benzyl alcohol; the other is oxidised to sodium benzoate.

Answer: Cannizzaro reaction: 2 C6H5CHO → C6H5CH2OH + C6H5COONa.

examples.problem: Which of these give a positive iodoform test: ethanal, propanal, propan-2-ol, acetone? Explain.
examples.solution:
1. Iodoform forms from a CH3CO– group or a CH3CH(OH)– group (which is first oxidised to it).
  2. Ethanal (CH3CHO) and acetone (CH3COCH3) have CH3CO– → positive.
  3. Propan-2-ol (CH3CH(OH)CH3) is oxidised to acetone → positive; propanal lacks the CH3CO group → negative.

Answer: Ethanal, acetone and propan-2-ol give positive; propanal is negative.

examples.problem: Distinguish between propanal and propanone using a chemical test.
examples.solution:
1. Propanal is an aldehyde (oxidisable); propanone is a ketone (not easily oxidised).
  2. Add Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO3) and warm.
  3. Propanal gives a silver mirror; propanone gives no reaction.

Answer: Tollens' test — propanal forms a silver mirror, propanone does not. (Fehling's also works for the aliphatic aldehyde.)

examples.problem: Name the reagents for converting acetone to propane (the –CH<sub>2</sub>– level) under acidic and under basic conditions.
examples.solution:
1. Reducing C=O fully to CH2 needs Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner.
  2. Acidic: Zn-Hg amalgam with concentrated HCl (Clemmensen reduction).
  3. Basic: hydrazine (NH2NH2) then KOH in ethylene glycol, heat (Wolff–Kishner).

Answer: Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) in acid; Wolff–Kishner (NH2NH2/KOH) in base — both give propane.

recap: The key reaction is nucleophilic addition: Nu attacks the δ+ carbon (sp<sup>2</sup> → sp<sup>3</sup>); examples are HCN (cyanohydrin), NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, alcohols (acetals), and NH<sub>2</sub>Z derivatives (oximes/hydrazones).
Aldehydes > ketones in reactivity (less steric hindrance and greater δ+); aldehydes oxidise easily, ketones do not.
Reduction: NaBH<sub>4</sub>/LiAlH<sub>4</sub> → alcohols; Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) and Wolff–Kishner (NH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>/KOH) → alkanes (–CH<sub>2</sub>–).
Compounds with α-H undergo aldol condensation (base) → β-hydroxy carbonyl → α,β-unsaturated product; those with no α-H undergo Cannizzaro (disproportionation) in conc. alkali.
Distinction: Tollens (silver mirror) and Fehling (red Cu<sub>2</sub>O) are positive for aldehydes; iodoform is positive for CH<sub>3</sub>CO– / CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)– compounds.

quiz.q: Which compound will NOT give the Cannizzaro reaction?
quiz.explanation: Cannizzaro needs an aldehyde with NO α-H. CH<sub>3</sub>CHO has α-H, so it does aldol instead.

quiz.q: A positive iodoform test is given by:
quiz.explanation: Acetophenone (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>) has a CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group, so it gives iodoform; the others do not.

quiz.q: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition mainly because of:
options: lower steric hindrance and higher δ+ on carbon
quiz.explanation: One small H and one R group make the aldehyde less hindered and more electrophilic.

quiz.q: Reduction of a ketone with NaBH<sub>4</sub> gives a:
quiz.explanation: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces C=O to C–OH; a ketone yields a secondary alcohol.

topics.title: Carboxylic Acids
topics.concept:
Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group –COOH (a carbonyl fused with a hydroxyl). The general formula of monocarboxylic acids is CnH2n+1COOH. The simplest is methanoic acid (HCOOH, formic acid) and the next is ethanoic acid (CH3COOH, acetic acid).

Nomenclature & structure

IUPAC names use the suffix -oic acid, numbering the carboxyl carbon as C-1 (CH3CH2COOH is propanoic acid; HOOC–COOH is ethanedioic/oxalic acid). The carboxyl carbon is sp2; both C–O bonds are intermediate between single and double because of resonance, so the group is planar. Carboxylic acids form strong intermolecular H-bonds (often as dimers), giving boiling points higher than alcohols of similar mass.

Methods of preparation

(a) Oxidation of 1° alcohols or aldehydes with KMnO4/K2Cr2O7 (e.g. CH3CH2OH → CH3COOH). (b) From nitriles and amides by acidic or basic hydrolysis (RCN + H2O/H+ → RCOOH). (c) From Grignard reagents + CO2: RMgX + CO2 → RCOOMgX, then H3O+ → RCOOH (adds one carbon). (d) From acyl halides/esters/anhydrides by hydrolysis. Oxidation of alkylbenzenes (KMnO4) gives benzoic acid.

Acidity

Carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols and phenols. On losing H+ they give the carboxylate ion, in which the negative charge is delocalised equally over two equivalent oxygens by resonance — a far greater stabilisation than the phenoxide ion enjoys. The strength is tuned by substituents: electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. –Cl, –NO2) stabilise the anion and increase acidity (so trichloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > chloroacetic acid > acetic acid), while electron-donating groups (alkyl, +I) decrease it. The closer the EWG is to –COOH and the more such groups present, the stronger the acid. A lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid.

Reactions

(a) Salt formation: with NaOH, Na2CO3 or NaHCO3 (effervescence of CO2 with bicarbonate distinguishes acids from phenols). (b) Formation of derivatives: with SOCl2/PCl5 → acid chloride; with an alcohol/H+ → ester (esterification); on heating with another acid molecule (loss of water, P4O10) → anhydride; with NH3 then heat → amide. (c) Reduction by LiAlH4 (or B2H6) gives a primary alcohol. (d) Decarboxylation: heating the sodium salt with soda-lime (NaOH/CaO) removes –COOH as CO2 to give an alkane (CH3COONa → CH4). (e) Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ): acids with an α-H react with Cl2/Br2 + red P to give α-halo acids. (f) Ring substitution: in benzoic acid the –COOH is deactivating and meta-directing, so halogenation/nitration occurs mainly at the m-position.

examples.problem: Arrange in increasing acid strength: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, ClCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, Cl<sub>2</sub>CHCOOH, Cl<sub>3</sub>CCOOH.
examples.solution:
1. Chlorine is electron-withdrawing (–I); it stabilises the carboxylate anion.
  2. More Cl atoms → greater stabilisation → stronger acid.
  3. So strength rises with the number of Cl atoms.

Answer: CH3COOH < ClCH2COOH < Cl2CHCOOH < Cl3CCOOH.

examples.problem: How can ethanoic acid be prepared from methyl magnesium bromide (CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr)?
examples.solution:
1. A Grignard reagent adds to CO2 (dry ice).
  2. CH3MgBr + CO2 → CH3COOMgBr.
  3. Acidic work-up (H3O+) gives CH3COOH.

Answer: CH3MgBr + CO2 → CH3COOMgBr ⟶(H3O+) CH3COOH (ethanoic acid).

examples.problem: Why is a carboxylic acid more acidic than the corresponding alcohol and phenol?
examples.solution:
1. Acidity depends on the stability of the anion left after losing H+.
  2. The carboxylate ion has its negative charge delocalised equally over two equivalent O atoms (strong resonance).
  3. An alkoxide has no such resonance; phenoxide has resonance into the ring but the charge ends on less electronegative carbons, so it is less stabilised.

Answer: The carboxylate anion is the most resonance-stabilised, so the carboxylic acid is the strongest of the three.

examples.problem: Identify the reagent that gives an acid chloride from a carboxylic acid, and write the reaction with ethanoic acid.
examples.solution:
1. SOCl2 (thionyl chloride) is preferred because the by-products (SO2, HCl) are gases.
  2. CH3COOH + SOCl2 → CH3COCl + SO2 + HCl.
  3. (PCl5 or PCl3 also work.)

Answer: SOCl2; CH3COOH → CH3COCl (acetyl chloride).

examples.problem: What is the product of heating sodium acetate with soda-lime? Name the reaction.
examples.solution:
1. Soda-lime (NaOH + CaO) on heating removes the –COOH group as CO2.
  2. CH3COONa + NaOH ⟶(CaO, Δ) CH4 + Na2CO3.
  3. This is decarboxylation.

Answer: Methane (CH4) by decarboxylation.

examples.problem: How would you distinguish ethanoic acid from phenol using a simple test?
examples.solution:
1. Carboxylic acids are stronger than carbonic acid; phenol is weaker.
  2. Add aqueous NaHCO3 to each.
  3. Ethanoic acid liberates CO2 (brisk effervescence); phenol gives no reaction.

Answer: NaHCO3 test — ethanoic acid gives CO2 effervescence, phenol does not.

recap: The carboxyl group –COOH has an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon and equivalent resonance-shared C–O bonds; acids exist as H-bonded dimers (high b.p.).
Preparation: oxidation of 1° alcohols/aldehydes, hydrolysis of nitriles/amides/esters, and Grignard + CO<sub>2</sub> (adds one carbon).
Acidity comes from the resonance-stabilised carboxylate; electron-withdrawing groups (–Cl, –NO<sub>2</sub>) raise acidity (lower $pK_a$), electron-donating groups lower it.

Reactions: salts (NaHCO<sub>3</sub> gives CO<sub>2</sub>, unlike phenol), acid chlorides (SOCl<sub>2</sub>), esters (ROH/H<sup>+</sup>), anhydrides, amides; reduction (LiAlH<sub>4</sub>) to 1° alcohols.
Decarboxylation (soda-lime) gives alkanes; HVZ gives α-halo acids; in benzoic acid –COOH is deactivating and meta-directing.

quiz.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so its –I effect stabilises the carboxylate most, giving the strongest acid.

quiz.q: Grignard reagent + CO<sub>2</sub> followed by acid hydrolysis gives a:
quiz.explanation: RMgX adds to CO<sub>2</sub> to give RCOOMgX, which on H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> gives RCOOH.

quiz.q: Which reagent best converts a carboxylic acid into an acid chloride?
quiz.explanation: SOCl<sub>2</sub> gives the acid chloride with gaseous by-products (SO<sub>2</sub>, HCl) that escape, leaving a pure product.

quiz.q: The carboxyl group on a benzene ring directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the:
quiz.explanation: –COOH is deactivating and meta-directing, so substitution occurs chiefly at the meta position.

online.title: Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids — Online Test

questions.q: The hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde is:
questions.explanation: Three coplanar sigma bonds and one pi bond mean sp<sup>2</sup>.

questions.q: Rosenmund reduction converts an acyl chloride into a(n):
questions.explanation: H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/BaSO<sub>4</sub> stops at the aldehyde.

questions.q: Which compound gives a positive iodoform test?
questions.explanation: Acetone has a CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group, so it gives CHI<sub>3</sub>.

questions.q: Tollens reagent is:
questions.explanation: Tollens reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate; aldehydes give a silver mirror.

questions.q: The strongest acid among the following is:
questions.explanation: Three –I chlorine atoms stabilise the anion most, so trichloroacetic acid is strongest.

questions.q: Which aldehyde undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction?
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde has no α-H and disproportionates in conc. alkali.

questions.q: Clemmensen reduction uses:
questions.explanation: Clemmensen uses zinc amalgam with concentrated HCl (acidic conditions).

questions.q: Addition of NaHSO<sub>3</sub> to acetaldehyde gives a:
questions.explanation: The bisulphite addition product is crystalline and used for purification.

questions.q: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition because of:
questions.explanation: Less crowding and a more electrophilic carbon make aldehydes more reactive.

questions.q: Grignard reagent + dry ice (CO<sub>2</sub>) then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> yields a:
questions.explanation: RMgX adds to CO<sub>2</sub> to give RCOOH after hydrolysis.

questions.q: Which reagent oxidises a primary alcohol only up to the aldehyde?
questions.explanation: PCC is mild and anhydrous, stopping at the aldehyde.

questions.q: The product of aldol condensation of acetaldehyde after dehydration is:
questions.explanation: 3-Hydroxybutanal loses water to give but-2-enal.

questions.q: Reaction of acetic acid with SOCl<sub>2</sub> gives:
questions.explanation: SOCl<sub>2</sub> converts –COOH to –COCl (acetyl chloride).

questions.q: Which test distinguishes an aliphatic aldehyde from an aromatic aldehyde?
questions.explanation: Fehling is positive only for aliphatic aldehydes; aromatic ones do not respond.

questions.q: The carboxyl group on a benzene ring is:
questions.explanation: –COOH withdraws electrons, deactivating the ring and directing meta.

questions.q: Which compound will NOT respond to Tollens test?
questions.explanation: Propanone is a ketone and does not reduce Tollens reagent.

questions.q: Wolff–Kishner reduction of cyclohexanone gives:
questions.explanation: NH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>/KOH reduces C=O fully to CH<sub>2</sub>, giving cyclohexane.

questions.q: Which has the lowest $pK_a$ (strongest acid)?
questions.explanation: Formic acid (no electron-donating alkyl group) is the strongest of these and has the lowest $pK_a$; phenol is much weaker.

questions.q: Acetals are formed by addition of which nucleophile to a carbonyl?
questions.explanation: Two equivalents of alcohol with dry HCl give an acetal (a protecting group).

questions.q: A 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) test is used to detect:
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP gives an orange precipitate with aldehydes and ketones (the >C=O group).

imo.title: Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids — Olympiad Test

questions.q: In nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, the geometry change at the attacked carbon is:
questions.explanation: The planar sp<sup>2</sup> carbon becomes tetrahedral sp<sup>3</sup> as the nucleophile adds.

questions.q: Which pair will both give a positive iodoform test?
questions.explanation: Both acetone and ethanal carry the CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group.

questions.q: A compound C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O gives a silver mirror with Tollens. It is:
questions.explanation: Only the aldehyde (propanal) reduces Tollens reagent; acetone (also C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O) does not.

questions.q: Increasing order of acidity: I CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, II ClCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, III FCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, IV CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH:
questions.explanation: Propanoic acid (extra +I) is weakest, then acetic acid, then ClCH<sub>2</sub>COOH, and FCH<sub>2</sub>COOH strongest (F most electronegative).

questions.q: X gives Cannizzaro but not aldol. X could be:
questions.explanation: HCHO has no α-H, so it cannot do aldol but undergoes Cannizzaro.

questions.q: Cross-aldol of benzaldehyde and acetaldehyde gives mainly:
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde has no α-H; the enolate of ethanal adds, then dehydration gives cinnamaldehyde.

questions.q: A carbonyl compound that does NOT undergo nucleophilic addition with NaHSO<sub>3</sub> readily is:
questions.explanation: The very bulky tert-butyl groups block the carbon sterically, so the bulky bisulphite cannot add.

questions.q: Identify the reagent: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> in basic medium:
questions.explanation: Full reduction of C=O to CH<sub>2</sub> in base is the Wolff–Kishner reaction.

questions.q: An acid C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub> liberates CO<sub>2</sub> with NaHCO<sub>3</sub> and gives no iodoform. It is:
questions.explanation: Acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) is acidic (CO<sub>2</sub> with bicarbonate) and has no CH<sub>3</sub>CO– oxidisable to iodoform.

questions.q: On ozonolysis, an alkene gives only propanone. The alkene is:
questions.explanation: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> cleaves into two molecules of propanone.

questions.q: Which conversion needs Grignard + CO<sub>2</sub> rather than simple oxidation?
questions.explanation: Going from a halide to an acid with one extra carbon requires CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + CO<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: In the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, the halogen is introduced at the:
questions.explanation: HVZ replaces an α-hydrogen of the acid with a halogen.

questions.q: Which will react fastest with HCN?
questions.explanation: Methanal is the least hindered and most electrophilic, so it adds HCN fastest.

questions.q: Esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is catalysed by H<sup>+</sup> and is best driven forward by:
options: removing water or using excess alcohol
questions.explanation: Esterification is reversible; removing water (or excess alcohol) shifts equilibrium to the ester.
